'''Sophie Willock Bryant''' (15 February 1850 – 14 August 1922) was an [[Anglo-Irish]] [[mathematician]], [[educator]], [[feminist]] and [[activist]].<ref name="NLCS">{{cite book|title=Sophie Bryant, D.Sc., Litt.D. 1850–1922|date=1922|publisher=North London Collegiate School|url=http://nlcsarchives.daisy.websds.net/PDFFiles/MemorialBooks/NLCSMBK0009.pdf|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20161024225840/http://nlcsarchives.daisy.websds.net/PDFFiles/MemorialBooks/NLCSMBK0009.pdf|archivedate=24 October 2016}}</ref> She was the first woman to receive a DSc in England; one of the first to serve on a Royal Commission and on the Senate of the University of London.

== Early life and education ==
Bryant was born Sophie Willock in Dublin in 1850. Her father was Revd Dr William Willock DD, Fellow and Tutor of [[Trinity College, Dublin]].
She was educated at home, largely by her father. As a teenager she moved to [[London]], when her father was appointed Professor of Geometry at the [[University of London]] in 1863, and she attended [[Bedford College (London)|Bedford College]]. At the age of nineteen she married Dr William Hicks Bryant, a surgeon ten years older than she was, who died of [[cirrhosis]] within a year.<ref name="ID1">{{cite news |url=http://www.irishdemocrat.co.uk/anonn-is-anall/sophie-bryant-1/ |author=Peter Berresford Ellis |title=Sophie Bryant (part 1) |date=10 December 2008 |newspaper=Irish Democrat |publisher=Connolly Publications Ltd |access-date=16 November 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081006111020/http://www.irishdemocrat.co.uk/anonn-is-anall/sophie-bryant-1/ |archive-date=6 October 2008  }}</ref><ref name="MT">{{MacTutor|title=Sophie Willock Bryant|id=Bryant}}</ref>

== Career ==
[[file:Frances Mary Buss and Mrs Sophie Bryant.jpg|thumb|Frances Mary Buss and Sophie Bryant]]
In 1875 Bryant became a teacher and was invited by [[Frances Mary Buss]] to join the staff of [[North London Collegiate School]]. In 1895 she succeeded Miss Buss as headmistress of [[North London Collegiate]], serving until 1918.<ref name="ID1"/><ref name="MT"/>

When the University of London opened its degree courses to women in 1878, she started attending.   In 1881, she became one of the first women to obtain a First Class Honours degree, in her case a BSc, in the first year that a British university awarded degrees to women.  This was in Mental and Moral Sciences (Philosophy).  She was awarded second class honours in mathematics. In 1884, she was awarded the degree of [[Doctor of Science#The United Kingdom.2C Ireland.2C India and the Commonwealth|Doctor of Science]] in Mental and Moral Sciences.  In 1882 she was the third woman to be elected to the [[London Mathematical Society]], and was the first active female member, publishing her first paper with the Society in 1884.<ref name="ID1"/><ref name="MT"/> Together with Charles Smith, Bryant edited three volumes of [[Euclid]]'s [[Euclid's Elements|Elements of Geometry]], for the use of schools (''Euclid's Elements of Geometry, books I and II'' (1897); ''Euclid's Elements of Geometry, books III and IV'' (1899); ''Euclid's Elements of Geometry, books VI and IX'' (1901)).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/008884920|title=Catalog Record: Euclid's elements of geometry: books I-IV, VI and XI|last=|first=|date=|website=HathiTrust Digital Library|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171024043204/https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/008884920|archive-date=24 October 2017|url-status=live|access-date=20 July 2017}}</ref>

Sophie Bryant was a pioneer in education for women. She was the first woman to receive a DSc in England; one of the first three women to be appointed to a [[Royal Commission]], the [[Royal Commission on Secondary Education|Bryce commission]] on Secondary Education in 1894–1895<ref>{{cite web |title=List of commissions and officials: 1890-1899 (nos. 73-102) Office-Holders in Modern Britain: Volume 10, Officials of Royal Commissions of Inquiry 1870-1939. |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/office-holders/vol10/pp27-42 |website=British History Online |publisher=UCL, London, 1995 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>; and one of the first three women to be appointed to the Senate of the University of London. When Trinity College Dublin opened its degrees to women, Bryant was one of the first to be awarded an honorary doctorate.<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Parkes |editor-first=Susan M. | first=Susan M.| last=Parkes| date=2004 |title=A Danger to the Men? A History of Women in Trinity College Dublin 1904-2004 |location=Dublin |publisher=Lilliput Press |chapter=The First Decade, 1904-1914L A Quiet Revolution |isbn=978-1-84351-040-6}}</ref> She was also instrumental in setting up the Cambridge Training College for Women, now [[Hughes Hall, Cambridge]].<ref name="ID1"/><ref name="MT"/> She is also said to have been one of the first women to own a [[bicycle]].<ref name="ID1"/>

While in London, she was a member of the London Ethical Society, an early [[secular humanist|humanist]] community which advocated moral living independent of religion.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://heritage.humanists.uk/sophie-bryant/|work=Humanist Heritage|publisher=[[Humanists UK]]|accessdate=7 January 2022|title=Sophie Bryant}}</ref> She was interested in Irish politics, wrote books on Irish history and ancient Irish law (''Celtic Ireland'' (1889), ''The Genius of the Gael'' (1913)), and was an ardent Irish nationalist from a Protestant family background. She was president of the Irish [[National Literary Society]] in 1914. She supported [[women's suffrage]] but advocated postponement until women were better educated.<ref name="ID1"/><ref name="MT"/><ref name="MT2">{{cite news |url=http://www.irishdemocrat.co.uk/anonn-is-anall/sophie-bryant-2/ |author=Peter Berresford Ellis |title=Sophie Bryant (part 2) |date=10 December 2008 |newspaper=Irish Democrat |publisher=Connolly Publications Ltd |access-date=16 November 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081001065009/http://www.irishdemocrat.co.uk/anonn-is-anall/sophie-bryant-2/ |archive-date=1 October 2008  }}</ref> She serve on consultative committees of the national Board of Education with other suffragists like [[Isabel Cleghorn]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Goodman |first1=Joyce |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF6GAgAAQBAJ&dq=Isabel+Cleghorn+-gaskell&pg=PA162 |title=Women, Educational Policy-Making and Administration in England: Authoritative Women Since 1800 |last2=Harrop |first2=Sylvia |page=162|date=1 November 2002 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-63970-0 |language=en}}</ref>

== Later life and death ==
Bryant loved physical activity and the outdoors. She rowed, cycled, and swam, and twice climbed the [[Matterhorn]].<ref name="RB1">{{cite news |url=http://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/people/sophie-bryant-mathematician-and-pioneer-of-education-for-women-1.2764635 |author=Rosita Boland |title=Sophie Bryant, mathematician and pioneer of education for women |date=23 August 2016 |newspaper=Irish Times |access-date=23 August 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160824145430/http://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/people/sophie-bryant-mathematician-and-pioneer-of-education-for-women-1.2764635 |archive-date=24 August 2016  }}</ref> She died in a hiking accident in the [[Alps]] in 1922, aged 72.<ref name="ID1"/><ref name="MT"/>
